analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals from suing for homes, garnishing wages, or hounding patients over medical debt, and funds buying up patient medical bills.
analysis.headline: The Patient Debt Relief Act was introduced in February 2026 with 18 cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no hearings, votes, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would use Medicare as leverage: any hospital that wants to keep participating would have to screen patients for charity care, offer appeals before collecting, cap repayment plans at 4% of a patient's monthly income, and stop putting liens on homes, garnishing wages, charging interest to low-income patients, or dumping medical debt on collectors. It would also create a $100 million grant program so a nonprofit can buy up and erase medical debt for people whose bills exceed 5% of their income or who earn under four times the poverty line. Hospitals that don't comply could face fines of up to $1 million per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who owe hospital bills — especially low- and middle-income households. Millions of Americans carry medical debt, and the bill would shield them from the harshest collection tools: home liens, wage garnishment, interest charges if they earn under 250% of the poverty line, and having their debt sold to collectors before being offered an affordable repayment plan capped at 4% of monthly income. Hospitals would also have to tell patients about financial assistance and screen every patient for it before billing. The grant program would directly erase debt for people whose medical debt exceeds 5% of their income or who earn up to 400% of the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals in Medicare could no longer put a lien on or foreclose on a patient's home to collect a medical bill.

Hospitals could not garnish patients' wages to collect medical debt, and before selling debt to a collector they would have to offer a repayment plan with monthly payments capped at 4% of the patient's gross monthly income.
For patients with household income at or below 250% of the poverty line, hospitals could not charge interest on medical debt and could not sell it to a collector at all.
Hospitals would have to screen patients for financial assistance, decide eligibility before collection, and let patients appeal denials; every bill would have to explain the patient's rights.
A new $100 million federal grant program would fund a nonprofit to buy up and wipe out medical debt of people whose debt exceeds 5% of their income or who earn up to 400% of the poverty line.
Hospitals face civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation, and a public portal would let patients report hospitals that break the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would lose collection tools (liens, garnishment, interest, rapid debt sales) and face fines up to $1 million per violation, plus the administrative cost of screening and appeals. Taxpayers fund the $100 million debt-relief grant program. Debt collectors would face a restricted market for buying medical debt.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is enforced mainly through after-the-fact civil monetary penalties, 90-day notices, and annual audits of only a random sample of hospitals starting in 2029, so noncompliant hospitals could operate for years before facing consequences.
The bill does not cap what hospitals can charge or bill in the first place — it only restricts how debt is collected afterward, so the underlying size of medical bills is untouched.

The debt buyout program relies on a single nonprofit grantee, which could limit how quickly or broadly debts are acquired and discharged, and funding ($100 million) would cover only a fraction of outstanding medical debt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to patients are concrete and the costs fall mainly on hospitals' collection revenues and on taxpayers through a $100 million grant program. The main weakness is design: enforcement relies on after-the-fact penalties and audits rather than direct federal rules, and the debt-relief grant goes to a single nonprofit intermediary, which could be slow or limited in reach. Still, the collection restrictions address practices that push families into bankruptcy, and the cost to hospitals is small relative to their operating budgets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in February 2026, and with no committee action since, it sits there until the Congress ends.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2026, and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
The full action history after the referrals is empty: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital groups and medical debt collectors are better off so far, because the restrictions on liens, wage garnishment, and debt sales have not advanced and would never take effect if the bill dies in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and debt collectors, so far

for.name: Rep. Gabe Vasquez
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce/Ways and Means jurisdictions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 10, 2026, tying hospital collection rules to Medicare participation.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record, though the bill has not yet reached any vote where party positions would be tested.

industries.note: Hospitals would lose their most aggressive collection tools — home liens, wage garnishment, interest on low-income patients' bills, and quick sales of debt to collectors — and face fines up to $1 million per violation for noncompliance. The restrictions are conditioned on Medicare participation, so no hospital could keep them and still treat Medicare patients.

industries.industry: Medical debt collectors and debt buyers
industries.note: Collectors could only buy medical debt a year or more after it was due, only from patients who declined or dropped a capped repayment plan, and only under the same no-lien, no-garnishment rules — shrinking both the volume and the profitability of medical debt collection.

The bill authorizes $100 million in grants to a nonprofit mission-built to buy and discharge patient medical debt, giving the existing medical debt forgiveness model a large new federal revenue stream.

analysis.trajectory: First-term-member bills with no cosponsors from the majority party that sit in two committees with no hearings rarely reach the House floor; unless a committee schedules a markup or the debt-relief provisions get attached to a larger health package, this bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
